resources.title: 4.2 Cardiac Muscle & Electrical Activity
resources.content:
# 4.2 Cardiac Muscle & Electrical Activity ## Learning objectives By the end of this note, you should be able to: - explain how cardiac muscle is organised as a functional syncytium; - describe the ionic basis of the ventricular action potential; - distinguish fast-response contractile cells from slow-response nodal cells; - explain excitation–contraction coupling and Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release; - relate refractory periods to the inability of normal cardiac muscle to tetanise; - explain how autonomic stimulation changes cardiac rate and contractility. ## 1. The heart as an electrical and mechanical organ Cardiac function depends on two linked events: Electrical activation → Ca²⁺ mobilisation → mechanical contraction The myocardium is specialised to generate rhythmic electrical activity, conduct that activity through the heart, and convert it into coordinated contraction. Cardiac muscle cells are branched and striated. Adjacent cells are connected by intercalated discs, which provide both mechanical attachment and electrical coupling. Gap junctions permit current to spread from cell to cell, allowing groups of cells to behave as a functional syncytium. Two broad cell populations are physiologically important: | Property | Contractile myocytes | Pacemaker/conducting cells | | --- | --- | --- | | Main role | Generate force | Generate or conduct electrical activity | | Stable resting potential | Yes, approximately −90 mV in ventricular cells | No fixed resting potential in dominant pacemaker cells | | Upstroke mechanism | Mainly rapid Na⁺ influx | Mainly Ca²⁺ influx in nodal tissue | | Plateau | Prominent in ventricular myocytes | Not prominent in nodal cells | | Spontaneous depolarisation | Normally absent | Present in pacemaker tissue | --- ## 2. Ventricular contractile-cell action potential The ventricular action potential is long compared with that of a typical neuron. Its prolonged duration is central to cardiac physiology. ### 2.1 Phase 4 — resting membrane potential Ventricular cells maintain a resting membrane potential near −90 mV, largely because resting K⁺ permeability is high and the equilibrium potential for K⁺ is strongly negative. The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase maintains the transmembrane Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients that make this electrical behaviour possible. ### 2.2 Phase 0 — rapid depolarisation A threshold stimulus opens fast voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. Na⁺ rapidly enters the cell, producing a steep upstroke and driving the membrane potential toward positive values. ### 2.3 Phase 1 — initial repolarisation Fast Na⁺ channels become inactivated. A brief outward K⁺ current produces a small early fall in membrane potential. ### 2.4 Phase 2 — plateau The plateau is the defining feature of the ventricular action potential. During this phase: - L-type Ca²⁺ channels allow sustained Ca²⁺ entry; - outward K⁺ currents oppose this inward current; - the membrane therefore remains depolarised for a prolonged period. The plateau links electrical activity to contraction because the entering Ca²⁺ acts as the trigger for further Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. ### 2.5 Phase 3 — repolarisation Ca²⁺ channels progressively inactivate while K⁺ efflux becomes dominant. The membrane returns toward its resting potential. The sequence can be simplified as: Na⁺ in → brief K⁺ out → Ca²⁺ in + K⁺ out → K⁺ out → rest --- ## 3. Cardiac excitation–contraction coupling A ventricular action potential does not directly pull actin and myosin together. It first changes intracellular Ca²⁺ availability. The functional sequence is: Action potential → L-type Ca²⁺ channel opening → small Ca²⁺ influx → ryanodine receptor activation → SR Ca²⁺ release → ↑ cytosolic Ca²⁺ → troponin C binding → tropomyosin displacement → cross-bridge cycling → contraction This is called Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release (CICR). The extracellular Ca²⁺ entry is therefore a trigger, not the sole source of Ca²⁺ used for contraction. ### 3.1 Relaxation Relaxation requires the cytosolic Ca²⁺ concentration to fall. Major mechanisms include: - SERCA pumping Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum; - Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange (NCX) moving Ca²⁺ out of the cell; - a smaller contribution from the plasma-membrane Ca²⁺ ATPase. The rate of Ca²⁺ removal affects both relaxation and the Ca²⁺ available for subsequent beats. --- ## 4. Refractory periods The ventricular action potential produces a long absolute refractory period followed by a relative refractory period. During the absolute refractory period, another normal action potential cannot be initiated because the fast Na⁺ channels are unavailable for reactivation. This prolonged refractory period overlaps most of mechanical systole. ### Why this matters Cardiac muscle normally cannot produce sustained tetanus. The heart therefore has time to: contract → eject → relax → refill This is essential for continuous pumping. --- ## 5. Nodal tissue and pacemaker activity The sinoatrial node and other nodal tissues differ from ventricular myocytes. The dominant pacemaker cells do not maintain a truly stable resting membrane potential. Instead, after repolarisation they undergo gradual spontaneous depolarisation during phase 4. ### 5.1 Simplified pacemaker cycle Phase 4 spontaneous depolarisation → threshold → Ca²⁺-dependent upstroke → K⁺-mediated repolarisation → phase 4 again A major current contributing to the gradual depolarisation is the funny current (If), with important contributions from other inward and outward currents. The rate at which phase 4 reaches threshold determines pacemaker firing frequency. ### 5.2 Dominant pacemaker principle The SA node normally has the fastest spontaneous rate and therefore suppresses slower latent pacemakers by overdrive suppression. If SA-node activity fails, other regions of the conduction system can generate escape rhythms at slower rates. --- ## 6. Autonomic modulation The autonomic nervous system does not normally create the heart's basic rhythm; it modulates the intrinsic rhythm. ### Sympathetic stimulation β₁-adrenoceptor activation increases cAMP-dependent signalling and generally causes: - increased phase 4 slope in pacemaker cells; - increased heart rate (positive chronotropy); - increased AV nodal conduction (positive dromotropy); - increased contractility (positive inotropy); - increased relaxation rate (positive lusitropy). ### Parasympathetic stimulation Vagal activation, primarily through M₂ receptors, generally causes: - reduced pacemaker slope; - increased K⁺ conductance and membrane hyperpolarisation; - reduced heart rate; - slowed AV nodal conduction. Parasympathetic influence is strongest at the SA and AV nodes and is relatively limited in ventricular myocardium. --- ## 7. The force–calcium relationship The force generated by cardiac muscle depends on the amount of activator Ca²⁺ and the sensitivity of the contractile apparatus to Ca²⁺. Increasing intracellular Ca²⁺ generally increases the number of activated cross-bridges and therefore increases force. β₁ stimulation enhances Ca²⁺ entry and SR Ca²⁺ cycling, explaining why sympathetic stimulation increases contractility. This also demonstrates why electrical, ionic and mechanical physiology must be learned together: the ECG reflects electrical activity, but the clinical consequence of that electrical activity is ultimately determined by Ca²⁺ handling and mechanical performance. --- ## 8. Clinical integration Hyperkalaemia: a reduced K⁺ gradient can depolarise the resting membrane potential and alter excitability and conduction. Severe disturbances can produce dangerous rhythm abnormalities. Calcium-channel blockers: drugs that inhibit L-type Ca²⁺ channels can reduce contractility and/or slow AV nodal conduction depending on the agent. β-blockers: reducing β₁-mediated signalling lowers sympathetic effects on rate, conduction and contractility. Ischaemia: altered membrane energetics, extracellular K⁺, ATP availability and ion handling can produce abnormal electrical activity and impaired contractility. Arrhythmias: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity or re-entry can disturb coordinated cardiac excitation. --- ## 9. High-yield synthesis - Cardiac muscle is electrically coupled through gap junctions and mechanically linked at intercalated discs. - Ventricular myocytes have a long action potential with a Ca²⁺-dependent plateau. - The plateau permits Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release from the SR. - Cardiac contraction uses troponin C, not the smooth-muscle calmodulin/MLCK system. - The long refractory period prevents normal tetany. - SA-node cells show spontaneous phase 4 depolarisation and normally determine heart rate. - Sympathetic stimulation increases rate, conduction and contractility; parasympathetic stimulation mainly slows the SA/AV nodes. - The clinically important chain is electrical event → Ca²⁺ event → mechanical event. ## References - OpenStax, Anatomy and Physiology 2e, cardiovascular and muscle physiology chapters. - Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology, cardiac muscle and cardiac electrophysiology. - Costanzo, Physiology, cardiovascular physiology. - Ganong, Review of Medical Physiology, cardiac electrophysiology and excitation–contraction coupling. ## 10. Active recall 1. Why does ventricular cardiac muscle have a plateau phase? 2. Explain calcium-induced calcium release. 3. Why is the cardiac refractory period important? 4. Distinguish ventricular myocyte action potentials from SA-node pacemaker potentials. 5. What is the role of gap junctions in cardiac muscle? 6. How do beta-adrenergic signals alter rate and contractility? 7. Why can altered extracellular potassium affect cardiac conduction? 8. Link an electrical change to a possible mechanical consequence. ## 11. Flashcards - Q: What structure electrically couples adjacent cardiac myocytes? A: Gap junctions in intercalated discs. - Q: What ion contributes to the ventricular action-potential plateau? A: Calcium entering through L-type calcium channels, balanced by outward currents. - Q: What triggers calcium-induced calcium release? A: Calcium entry triggers additional calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. - Q: Which protein binds calcium to initiate cardiac thin-filament regulation? A: Troponin C. - Q: Why does cardiac muscle resist tetany? A: Its long action potential and refractory period prevent repeated summation like skeletal muscle. - Q: What is characteristic of SA-node phase 4? A: Spontaneous diastolic depolarisation. - Q: What does beta-1 stimulation generally do? A: Increases heart rate, conduction and contractility through cAMP-related signalling. - Q: What does parasympathetic stimulation chiefly slow? A: SA-node rate and AV-node conduction. ## 12. MCQs

1. The ventricular action-potential plateau depends importantly on: A. L-type calcium current. B. Complete absence of ion movement. C. Chloride only. D. Haemoglobin binding.

Answer: A. Calcium entry helps sustain the plateau and supports excitation–contraction coupling.

2. Calcium-induced calcium release means: A. Calcium entry triggers further calcium release from the SR. B. Sodium directly forms myosin. C. ATP is not needed for contraction. D. The nucleus releases calcium into blood.

Answer: A. Trigger calcium activates SR calcium release channels.

3. The long cardiac refractory period is important because it: A. Prevents normal sustained tetany. B. Stops every heartbeat. C. Eliminates the need for calcium. D. Makes cardiac cells identical to neurons.

Answer: A. Refractoriness allows relaxation and filling between contractions.

4. Spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation is characteristic of: A. SA-node pacemaker cells. B. Mature erythrocytes. C. Tendons. D. Platelets only.

Answer: A. Pacemaker currents and calcium currents help bring SA-node cells to threshold.

5. Which protein binds calcium in the cardiac contractile regulatory complex? A. Troponin C. B. Albumin. C. Collagen. D. Fibrinogen.

Answer: A. Calcium binding to troponin C permits thin-filament regulatory changes.

6. Gap junctions are important because they: A. Permit electrical current between adjacent myocytes. B. Store bile. C. Carry oxygen in plasma. D. Replace all ion channels.

Answer: A. They help coordinate excitation across cardiac tissue.

7. Increased extracellular potassium can alter cardiac excitability because it changes: A. Potassium gradients and resting membrane potential. B. The amino-acid sequence of haemoglobin immediately. C. Bile flow. D. Bone mineralisation.

Answer: A. Changes in the K+ gradient can depolarise the resting potential and alter channel availability/conduction.

8. Which sequence best links excitation to contraction? A. Electrical activation → calcium entry/release → troponin regulation → force. B. Oxygen binding → bile secretion → force. C. Platelet plug → calcium loss → force. D. DNA replication → immediate contraction.

Answer: A. Cardiac mechanics depend on the calcium transient and myofilament activation. ## 13. Practical / ECG and physiology station Station: connect an electrical event to contraction (8 minutes; 12 marks) 1. Identify the broad phases of a ventricular action potential on a provided graph (4 marks). 2. Mark the plateau and state the role of L-type calcium channels (2 marks). 3. Explain how the calcium transient initiates contraction (2 marks). 4. Explain why the refractory period prevents normal tetany (2 marks). 5. State one effect of sympathetic beta-1 stimulation (2 marks). ## 14. Calculation / graph interpretation For a regular rhythm, an introductory estimate of heart rate from an ECG is heart rate (beats/min) = 60 ÷ R–R interval in seconds. Example: an R–R interval of 0.8 s gives 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats/min. This shortcut assumes a regular rhythm; irregular rhythms require a more appropriate counting method and full ECG interpretation. Graph task: identify rapid depolarisation, plateau and repolarisation on a ventricular action-potential graph. Do not infer mechanical output from the ECG alone. ## 15. Past-paper alignment Pattern-based only; verified Bowen past papers were not supplied. Prioritise ventricular versus pacemaker action potentials, L-type calcium channels, calcium-induced calcium release, troponin C, refractory period, autonomic effects, potassium disturbances and basic ECG rate interpretation. These are predicted assessment patterns, not confirmed historical questions. ## 16. Recommended resources - Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology — cardiac muscle and electrophysiology. - Costanzo, Physiology — action potentials and excitation–contraction coupling. - Ganong, Review of Medical Physiology — cardiac electrical activity. - A standard ECG practical guide for interval measurement and rhythm-rate exercises. ## 17. Final mastery review - [ ] I can distinguish ventricular myocyte and SA-node action potentials. - [ ] I can explain the calcium-dependent plateau and calcium-induced calcium release. - [ ] I can explain the long refractory period and its function. - [ ] I can connect troponin C activation to force development. - [ ] I can explain sympathetic and parasympathetic effects on the heart. - [ ] I can explain why potassium disturbances alter excitability. - [ ] I scored at least 7/8 MCQs and can justify every answer. - [ ] I can complete the graph station and calculate a regular rhythm rate.

resources.title: 3.1 Enzyme Structure, Active Sites & Specificity
resources.content: ## Learning objectives - Explain how enzyme structure determines catalytic function. - Define active site, substrate specificity and induced fit. - Distinguish enzymes from substrates and cofactors. - Relate enzyme dysfunction to clinical disease. ## 1. Enzymes as biological catalysts Enzymes accelerate biochemical reactions by lowering the activation-energy barrier. They do not change the overall equilibrium position of a reaction or become permanently consumed. Most enzymes are proteins, although some catalytic RNA molecules exist. ## 2. Active site The active site is the region of an enzyme where substrate binding and catalysis occur. Its three-dimensional shape and chemical environment determine which substrates can bind and how they are positioned for reaction. ## 3. Specificity and induced fit Enzyme specificity arises from complementary interactions between enzyme and substrate. The induced-fit model emphasises that substrate binding can alter enzyme conformation, creating a catalytic arrangement rather than requiring a perfectly rigid lock-and-key match. ## 4. Cofactors and coenzymes Some enzymes require non-protein components. Cofactors may be inorganic ions such as Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺. Coenzymes are organic molecules that participate in enzyme reactions; many are derived from vitamins. The protein component without its required cofactor is an apoenzyme; the complete active complex is a holoenzyme. ## 5. Clinical integration Mutations, deficiency of cofactors or toxic inhibition can reduce enzyme activity and disrupt metabolic pathways. Enzyme measurements in blood can also provide evidence of tissue injury because intracellular enzymes may enter the circulation after cell damage. ## Active Recall 1. What does an enzyme change in a reaction? 2. What does an enzyme not change about equilibrium? 3. What is an active site? 4. Why is induced fit more useful than a rigid lock-and-key model? 5. Distinguish cofactor and coenzyme. 6. Define apoenzyme and holoenzyme. 7. Why can plasma enzyme measurements indicate tissue injury? ## Exam Traps - Enzymes lower activation energy; they do not make an otherwise impossible equilibrium magically favourable. - Enzymes do not permanently shift the equilibrium position. - Not every cofactor is a coenzyme; inorganic ions are cofactors but not coenzymes. - Specificity depends on three-dimensional chemical complementarity, not shape alone. ## Visual Build Brief Show enzyme + substrate binding, induced conformational change, catalytic conversion and product release. Add a small inset comparing apoenzyme and holoenzyme. ## One-Minute Map 3D enzyme structure → active site → substrate recognition → induced fit → catalysis → metabolic function → clinical relevance. ## References - Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry. - Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry. - Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry. ## Assessment and mastery layer ### Mechanisms and relationships: quick synthesis - Primary sequence: amino-acid sequence → folding and subunit assembly → active-site geometry and chemistry → substrate recognition → transition-state stabilisation → product formation. - Induced fit is dynamic: substrate binding can reposition catalytic residues and exclude water or other molecules where appropriate. - Specificity is determined by complementary shape, charge, hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonding and catalytic chemistry—not shape alone. - A required metal ion or organic cofactor may participate in substrate binding, charge stabilisation or electron transfer. Removing a required cofactor can reduce activity without changing the enzyme's amino-acid sequence. - A mutation can disrupt folding, stability, active-site residues, oligomerisation or intracellular targeting; the clinical effect depends on the enzyme and tissue/pathway involved. ### Clinical integration - Inherited enzyme dysfunction: a variant can reduce catalytic activity, stability or correct localisation. The resulting pattern may include substrate accumulation, product deficiency or diversion into alternative pathways. - Cofactor deficiency: a vitamin-derived coenzyme may become limiting even when the enzyme protein is present. Distinguish this from a primary structural mutation. - Denaturation: extreme temperature, pH or chemical exposure may disrupt conformation and reduce function; mild changes can be reversible, while extensive denaturation may not be. - Laboratory interpretation: measured enzyme activity depends on enzyme quantity, catalytic efficiency, sample handling, temperature, pH and assay design. Do not equate one low activity result automatically with an inherited disorder. ### Exam recognition: common traps - Enzymes lower activation energy; they do not change the reaction's equilibrium constant. - The active site includes substrate-binding and catalytic features; not every binding site is catalytic. - Induced fit allows conformational adjustment after binding. - Apoenzyme = protein component without its required cofactor; holoenzyme = functional enzyme–cofactor complex. - A coenzyme is an organic cofactor; a metal ion is a cofactor but not a coenzyme. - Specificity is not absolute in every enzyme: some enzymes act on related substrates, and physiological context affects apparent specificity. ### Flashcards 1. Q: What determines an enzyme's substrate specificity? A: Complementary active-site shape, chemical interactions and catalytic arrangement. 2. Q: What is induced fit? A: Substrate binding promotes a conformational change that improves the catalytic arrangement. 3. Q: What does an enzyme lower? A: Activation free energy. 4. Q: Does an enzyme change equilibrium constant? A: No. 5. Q: Define apoenzyme. A: The protein component without a required cofactor. 6. Q: Define holoenzyme. A: The functional enzyme complex with its required cofactor(s). 7. Q: What is a coenzyme? A: An organic cofactor that participates in enzyme catalysis. 8. Q: How can a mutation reduce enzyme function without changing the catalytic residue directly? A: It may disrupt folding, stability, assembly or intracellular targeting. 9. Q: Why can vitamin deficiency impair an enzyme reaction? A: It can reduce availability of a required vitamin-derived coenzyme. 10. Q: Why is low measured activity not automatically proof of inherited disease? A: Activity is affected by enzyme quantity, assay conditions, sample handling and acquired factors. ### Original MCQs 1. The main energetic effect of an enzyme is to: A. Lower activation free energy B. Change the equilibrium constant C. Make every reaction exergonic D. Change the net stoichiometry. Answer: A. Catalysis changes the reaction rate, not the equilibrium position. 2. The induced-fit model emphasises: A. A rigid enzyme that never changes shape B. Conformational adjustment after substrate binding C. Permanent consumption of enzyme D. Inhibition by every substrate. Answer: B. 3. An apoenzyme is: A. An enzyme plus all required cofactors B. The protein component lacking a required cofactor C. A product of catalysis D. A denatured substrate. Answer: B. 4. Which is an organic cofactor? A. NAD+ B. Zn2+ C. Mg2+ D. Fe2+ alone. Answer: A. NAD+ is an organic coenzyme; metal ions are inorganic cofactors. 5. A mutation distant from the active site may reduce activity by: A. Disrupting folding or stability B. Necessarily changing the equilibrium constant C. Converting the enzyme into a substrate D. Always increasing Vmax. Answer: A. 6. A reaction proceeds faster after an enzyme is added. Which statement is correct? A. The equilibrium constant must increase B. The activation barrier is lowered C. The products become permanently more stable D. The enzyme is irreversibly consumed. Answer: B. 7. A patient has low activity of a vitamin-dependent enzyme during a nutritional deficiency. The most appropriate first interpretation is: A. Cofactor availability may be limiting B. An inherited mutation is proven C. The enzyme has no active site D. Equilibrium has been abolished. Answer: A. 8. Enzyme specificity depends most directly on: A. Complementary binding and catalytic chemistry B. Molecular mass alone C. The colour of the enzyme D. The number of products alone. Answer: A. ### Practical and application stations - Station A — enzyme model (4 minutes): label the active site, substrate, catalytic residues and product; explain one induced-fit change. - Station B — cofactor comparison (4 minutes): classify Mg2+, Zn2+, NAD+ and coenzyme A as cofactors/coenzymes and explain their possible catalytic roles. - Station C — pathway block (6 minutes): given a hypothetical enzyme defect, predict which substrate may accumulate, which product may fall and why alternative pathways may alter the pattern. - Station D — activity assay (5 minutes): identify at least three reasons measured enzyme activity may be low apart from an inherited structural defect. ### Past-paper alignment No authenticated Bowen examination paper was supplied for this page. Predicted assessment formats include definitions, enzyme–substrate diagrams, cofactor classification, induced-fit explanation and short metabolic-block vignettes. These are predicted formats, not verified historical questions. ### Resources - Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry — enzyme structure and function. - Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry — enzyme catalysis and coenzymes. - Nelson & Cox, Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry — protein structure and catalysis. - Bowen lecturer notes and the current course outline. ### Final review and mastery gate - [ ] I can explain how structure creates specificity. - [ ] I can distinguish induced fit from a rigid lock-and-key description. - [ ] I can explain activation energy versus equilibrium. - [ ] I can distinguish cofactor, coenzyme, apoenzyme and holoenzyme. - [ ] I can explain how mutations, denaturation and cofactor deficiency alter function. - [ ] I can score at least 7/8 MCQs and justify each answer. - [ ] I can complete three of four practical stations without notes. - [ ] I will revisit missed items after 24 hours and one week.
